articles.title: ASEAN economies grow but young graduates left behind - ABC Asia - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: ASEAN economies grow but young graduates left behind - ABC Asia  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Across South-East Asia, rapid economic growth has obscured a growing contradiction — while national economies continue to expand, many young people are struggling to achieve economic security, facing persistently high unemployment and a tightening labour market.
Addressing this disconnect requires evaluating how development is conventionally tracked.
ASEAN countries are experiencing respectable GDP growth rates — from 5.1 per cent in Indonesia to 8 eight per cent in Vietnam in 2025.
Yet youth outcomes have not matched the pace of overall growth.
Indonesian youth unemployment remained at 13.1 per cent in 2023, while in Vietnam it grew by 2.8 percentage points between 2010 and 2025 despite GDP per capita more than doubling across the same period.
University graduates feel the pain
High youth unemployment is even more perplexing when placed in the context of rising levels of educational attainment, driven by young people who increasingly pursue tertiary education in line with the conventional wisdom that it offers a path to social mobility.
Yet unemployment among tertiary graduates in the Philippines stood at 3.4 per cent in 2023, higher than the national rate of 2.4 per cent and the rate of 1.9 per cent among Filipinos with only a primary or lower secondary education.
This exemplifies the process of credential inflation, in which the growing supply of degrees outpaces the jobs that require them.
Unemployment statistics may also understate the problem, as jobs with basic social protections and opportunities for advancement are increasingly uncommon.
Informal employment makes up 68.5 per cent of Vietnam’s total workforce. Facing unemployment, some look outwards — 81 per cent of Filipino youth and 79 per cent of Thai youth under 30 expressed willingness to work abroad. This leaves governments with the difficult task of sustaining local employment.
Some academics blame the loss of formal jobs on a decline in manufacturing. In Indonesia, manufacturing value added as a percentage of GDP fell from 32 per cent in 2002 to 19.1 per cent in 2025.
This has negative consequences for labour market dynamics, leading to difficulties in job creation.
Yet the growing investment of ASEAN governments in manufacturing has not translated into a proportionate expansion of employment.
The Indonesian government’s 2020 nickel downstreaming strategy banned raw ore exports to encourage domestic smelting. Yet even as output increased, jobs fell.
The labour multiplier — a measure of the number of jobs supported by a given amount of final demand — decreased from approximately 6514 jobs per Rp 1 trillion ($A80 million) of final demand in 2010 to 3366 in 2016.
Vietnam also planned to invest in semiconductors but faced a severe shortage of skilled engineers.
More automation means fewer jobs
Labour demand shifts further complicate employment outcomes.
Much of the region’s new investment has moved towards capital- and technology-intensive industries that require fewer workers.
A 2018 survey of 150 Indonesian employers struggling to hire found 77 per cent cited the challenge of finding candidates with the desired qualifications.
The International Labour Organization warned ASEAN in 2016 that nearly three in five jobs in the region face a high risk of automation, with the risk reaching as high as 70 per cent in Vietnam.
Governments across ASEAN have begun implementing policies targeted at developing the skills needed for development under changing labour market conditions.
The Philippine government has received over $A1.4 billion in policy loans from the Asian Development Bank since 2017 to support initiatives promoting youth employment, including a program matching young people with internships, work and career guidance. Indonesia also launched its National Internship Program in October 2025.
The problem is that such programs focus on the resources they provide, without considering whether those resources will be converted into meaningful outcomes. An official evaluation of Indonesia’s policy in April 2026 revealed regional disparities and misaligned job roles.
What can be done?
To address the unemployment crisis, policy interventions should focus on converting economic growth into development.
National internship and training programs should focus on the competencies participants can demonstrate upon graduating. Work placement programs should also be designed to offer supervised training in professional judgement and workplace readiness, with skill certifications and reporting of employment outcomes.
Education policies should likewise be judged by the capabilities they build. Schooling must develop skills that will not be made redundant by automation.
With nearly three in five jobs across ASEAN at risk, public spending is better directed at the analytical and cross-disciplinary skills employers already report missing, since the expansion of tertiary education has outpaced the growth of graduate-level jobs.
Strategic investment should also prioritise industries that provide high-quality employment opportunities, a criterion capital-intensive sectors have consistently failed to meet.
Where a large proportion of the workforce is engaged in informal employment, such as in Vietnam, social protections for informal and underemployed workers can help ensure young people have the support to sustainably seek work and drive economic activity.
The ASEAN Qualifications Reference Framework, which enables comparisons of education qualifications across participating member states, could also turn ASEAN’s demographic imbalances into a shared advantage.
While more research is needed on how best to drive youth economic activity in South-East Asia, an over-reliance on GDP as a development proxy creates structural incentives to leave large portions of the population behind. Holistic understandings of development alongside growth must guide ASEAN’s future policymaking.

PHNOM PENH: The World Bank on Tuesday (Oct 6) downgraded Cambodia's 2026 economic growth forecast to 3.5 per cent, down from 5.3 per cent last year, citing a sharp slump in international tourist arrivals and surging fuel costs, reported Xinhua.
"In Cambodia, domestic demand weakened in 2026 as international arrivals and remittances fell, while higher oil prices squeezed household incomes," the bank said in its latest East Asia and Pacific Economic Update.
The report noted that while a real estate correction and tighter credit conditions weighed heavily on investment, overall growth was partially cushioned by rising goods exports.
The severe impact of energy costs is clearly reflected at local pumps. According to the Ministry of Commerce, the retail price of regular gasoline has risen to 5,150 riels (US$1.27) per litre on Tuesday, representing a 33.7 per cent increase compared to levels before the West Asia conflict. Meanwhile, diesel prices have climbed to 5,650 riels (US$1.39) per litre, marking a 46.7 per cent spike.
Over the medium term, Cambodia's economic growth is projected to rebound to four per cent in 2027 and five per cent in 2028, the report said.
This recovery is expected to be driven by stabilising energy prices, a revival in tourism, and the successful economic reintegration of returning migrant workers. However, the report cautioned that the El Nino weather phenomenon could temper the anticipated agricultural recovery in 2027.
The South-East Asian nation's economy remains heavily reliant on tourism, agriculture, real estate, construction, and the export of garments, textiles, footwear, and travel goods.
According to government data, exports of garments, textiles, footwear, and travel products rose 7.2 per cent year-on-year to US$11.76 billion during the first eight months of 2026. Conversely, international tourist arrivals plunged 44 per cent to 2.25 million over the same period, severely impacted by online scam issues, friction along the Cambodia-Thailand border and ongoing geopolitical conflicts in West Asia. - Bernama-Xinhua

Vietnamese banks are seeking to raise nearly $7 billion from foreign investors by the end of next year to sustain rapid economic growth and meet stricter capital requirements. The move comes as policymakers loosen foreign ownership limits and offshore borrowing caps amid a domestic funding squeeze.
Economic growth in communist-run Vietnam reached nearly 10% in the last quarter, driving heavy credit demand across the nation. The surge in lending has forced regulators to adjust strict access controls, which previously capped foreign ownership in domestic banks at 30% and restricted offshore borrowing.
Top leader To Lam's economic expansion drive has prompted authorities to allow greater foreign participation. The offshore borrowing ceiling was raised by 11% to $6.1 billion this year, while three local lenders received approval to increase foreign ownership limits to 49%.
Quynh Nguyen, a finance lecturer at Hoa Sen University in Ho Chi Minh City, noted that Vietnam is adjusting its approach to long-term funding while maintaining a targeted rollout.
"it is beginning to rethink how its next phase of growth will be financed," said Quynh Nguyen, finance lecturer at Hoa Sen University in Ho Chi Minh City.
She added that the recent share offers have generated renewed momentum among international strategic partners.
"particularly from strategic investors who are already familiar with Vietnam and are now considering deeper exposure," said Quynh Nguyen, finance lecturer at Hoa Sen University in Ho Chi Minh City.
Major state-owned and private institutions are currently leading the capital-raising wave. Vietcombank plans to sell a 6.5% stake worth $1.2 billion, while Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp is negotiating to increase its stake in VPBank to 20% through a $560 million private placement. BIDV sold a 3% stake in March and aims to unload another 11% by late next year.
Fitch Ratings analyst Willie Tanoto highlighted potential growth opportunities among smaller financial institutions in the region.
"We see some opportunities among the smaller banks to score some tie-ups down the line, provided Vietnam can maintain its growth story," said Willie Tanoto, analyst at Fitch Ratings.
The push for fresh capital is largely driven by rapid loan expansion and the transition to global Basel III standards by 2030. Rapid credit growth has particularly impacted the real estate sector, which represents a quarter of all bank loans and faces rising bad debts.
Fitch Ratings stated that the upcoming capital injections will primarily support immediate balance sheet expansion rather than significantly elevating capital buffers.

The credit rating agency pointed out that ongoing credit demands will necessitate continued investments from foreign financial entities over the coming years.

articles.summary: Singapore Passes Bill Giving MAS Powers to Set Loss Absorption Rules for D-SIBs  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
Singapore’s Parliament has passed a bill allowing the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to require banks deemed systemically important to hold additional resources that can absorb losses.
The Financial Services and Markets (Amendment) Bill passed on 6 October 2026.
In its second reading speech, MAS outlined plans to apply the Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) framework to Singapore’s Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs).
Banks Will Need More Resources to Absorb Losses
The framework will require D-SIBs to hold additional eligible loss-absorbing instruments and other financial resources to support their resolution if they become distressed.
MAS already has powers to bail in subordinated creditors of a distressed financial institution to restore its solvency.
The TLAC requirements will complement these powers by ensuring banks have resources available to absorb losses and help rebuild their capital.
MAS has consulted the industry and public on the required TLAC level, qualifying instruments and resources, public disclosures and the implementation timeline.
Under the amendments, MAS will be able to set these requirements and require institutions to disclose the level and composition of their TLAC, along with the priority of loss-absorbing instruments if they are wound up.
Institutions that fail to comply could face fines of up to S$250,000 upon conviction.
Continuing offences could attract additional fines of up to S$25,000 for each day or part of a day after conviction.
MAS noted that Singapore’s D-SIBs remain well-capitalised and well-managed.
It described the framework as part of ongoing efforts to prepare for the unlikely event of a distressed bank.
MAS Clarifies Its Role in Tackling Proliferation Financing
The bill also makes technical amendments to align Singapore’s counter-proliferation financing framework with updated Financial Action Task Force standards.
MAS’ existing anti-money laundering regime already requires financial institutions to mitigate risks linked to financing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. Its supervisory programme also covers these risks.
The amendments explicitly provide that MAS’ supervision covers proliferation financing alongside money laundering and terrorism financing.
They also clarify that MAS may assist domestic and foreign counterpart authorities in supervising proliferation financing risks.
Related changes cover other legislation administered by MAS.
The amendments will take effect on a date appointed by the minister through a gazette notification.

articles.full_text:
If you export a lot, how much profit do you retain?
 According to data from the General Statistics Office ( Ministry of Finance ), in September, the total value of goods exports and imports reached US$117.69 billion, an increase of 7.3% compared to the previous month and a 42.4% increase compared to the same period last year. The trade balance returned to a surplus after nine consecutive months of deficits, with a surplus of US$1.27 billion. However, looking at the first nine months of the year, Vietnam still had a trade deficit of US$19.42 billion, with exports reaching US$434.30 billion and imports totaling US$453.72 billion.
 The General Statistics Office considers this a fairly positive sign, but it is not enough to confirm that the trade deficit has ended. "The trade deficit of $19.42 billion is still a matter to monitor, because the rate of import growth is currently significantly higher than the rate of export growth. Some key export sectors, especially electronics, still largely depend on imported raw materials and components. The trade balance between the domestic economy and the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector shows a clear disparity, with one side experiencing a trade deficit and the other a trade surplus. This indicates limitations in input supply capacity, supporting industries, and a low domestic value-added ratio," a leader of the General Statistics Office analyzed. 
 Dr. Pham Viet Thuan, Director of the Institute of Resource and Environmental Economics in Ho Chi Minh City, also agrees that Vietnam returned to a trade surplus in September 2026, but overall, the economy is still in a trade deficit for the first nine months of 2026. This figure is completely contrary to the trade surplus of 16.87 billion USD in the same period of the previous year. It is noteworthy that behind the September trade surplus figure are contributions from two very different groups of driving forces. On one side is the processing and manufacturing industry, especially electronics, computers, components, and machinery and equipment, which generate a very large scale of exports, accounting for up to 80% of export turnover. On the other side is agriculture, forestry, and fisheries – a smaller group of goods but creating a more significant domestic surplus. Therefore, this figure needs to be evaluated realistically.
 It can be seen that, while agricultural, forestry, and fisheries exports may not be the largest in scale, they create a genuine trade surplus: Agriculture , forestry, and fisheries have a very large portion of their raw materials generated within the Vietnamese economy. Therefore, when these products are exported, a significant proportion of the revenue can be retained domestically in the form of income for farmers, processing businesses, labor, transportation, warehousing, and related services.
 Statistics from the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment show that in the past nine months, exports of agricultural, forestry, and aquatic products are estimated at approximately US$56.3 billion, an increase of 7.8% compared to the same period last year. In the first six months alone, this group of goods achieved US$35.88 billion in exports, while imports totaled around US$26.6 billion, resulting in a trade surplus of over US$9 billion. Meanwhile, some processing industries, especially electronics, may have very large export turnovers, but at the same time, the demand for imported components, raw materials, and machinery is also very high. Overall, in the first nine months, this group had the largest trade deficit, approximately US$65.28 billion.
 We need to increase the value of our exports.
 Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), analyzed: When a corporation invests in electronics, semiconductors, automobiles, energy, or technology in Vietnam, success needs to be measured by its linkages with domestic businesses and the transfer of skills and technology; training of domestic engineers and managers; and on-site research and development activities. Especially important is the improvement in productivity and competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses within that ecosystem. Vietnam needs to shift from a mindset of attracting FDI projects to building an ecosystem around FDI. This will create a significant spillover effect for the domestic economy. 
 The General Statistics Office believes that the trade outlook for the remaining months of the year may remain positive, but to establish a sustainable trade surplus trend, Vietnam needs to shift from aiming for higher exports to aiming for greater value retention. This will also be a decisive factor in determining the quality of export growth in the coming years.
 Economists generally agree that for a sustainable trade surplus, the goal should not only be to sell more, but also to retain more value. If this is achieved, every dollar of exports will generate more income for domestic producers, processing businesses, and service industries. Therefore, Vietnam's challenge in the remaining months of the year is not simply to maintain a monthly trade surplus, but to improve the quality of the trade balance. In other words, a sustainable trade surplus is not just about exporting more than importing, but about increasingly creating products using domestically sourced raw materials, technology, labor, and services. This will allow for the retention of a larger portion of export value within the domestic economy.
 In the long term, it is necessary to gradually develop supporting industries, increase the localization rate, and enhance the participation of Vietnamese businesses in the supply chains of FDI corporations.
 Mr. Bino Jacob, General Director of Nestlé Vietnam, gave a specific example: "As our investment in Vietnam grows, so does the capacity of Vietnamese businesses. Twelve years ago, we started cooperating with a small logistics company in Vietnam, Tuan Minh, based in Hanoi, which only had four trucks, and we were their only customer. Now, this company has five other multinational corporations as customers. From those four initial trucks, they now have over 50, meeting 60% of our total needs in the northern region. Whether it's packaging, logistics, or mobilizing engineering companies to come and build factories, all of this opens up opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate in the value chain and benefit together. This is the direction for Vietnamese goods to sustainably increase in value and drive many other developments."

articles.title: Singapore's Tech Workforce Hits 222,000 as Digital Economy Reaches 20% of GDP - https://www.briefasia.com/
articles.summary: Singapore's Tech Workforce Hits 222,000 as Digital Economy Reaches 20% of GDP  https://www.briefasia.com/
articles.full_text:
Tech Talent Migration Beyond Traditional Boundaries
Singapore's technology workforce expanded by 3.8 per cent to reach 222,000 professionals in 2025, according to data from the Infocomm Media Development Authority released on 5 October. The growth reflects a structural shift in where technical expertise is deployed across the economy, with traditional non-tech sectors now accounting for the majority of technology employment.
The digital economy reached S$144.1 billion in 2025, up from S$136.5 billion the previous year, representing 19.3 per cent of gross domestic product. This compares with 18.8 per cent in 2024, underscoring the Republic's continued transition towards digitally intensive economic activity.
Industries outside the information and communications sector employed 59 per cent of tech professionals, IMDA noted. Finance, manufacturing and other traditional sectors added 6,500 technology roles year-on-year, a 5.3 per cent increase that brought total tech employment in non-tech industries to 130,900. By contrast, the information and communications sector itself added just 1,700 positions, growing 1.8 per cent to 91,300.
Wage Premium and Occupational Patterns
Technology professionals now represent 5.4 per cent of Singapore's total workforce, up from 5.3 per cent in 2024 and 5.2 per cent in 2023. The median monthly wage for tech roles stood at S$8,000 in 2025, a marginal increase from S$7,950 the previous year. IMDA characterised this as significantly higher than the overall resident median of S$5,000.
Roles in artificial intelligence, data analytics and cybersecurity were among the fastest-growing occupations within the technology workforce, according to IMDA. The agency did not break out specific growth figures for these specialisations.
Digitalisation Value Concentrated in Legacy Sectors
The bulk of digital economy value addition stems from digitalisation efforts within non-tech sectors rather than from the information and communications sector itself. Digitalisation across manufacturing, finance, insurance and trade generated S$97 billion in nominal value-added in 2025, a 3.6 per cent increase from S$93.6 billion in 2024.
Finance and insurance led this segment at S$39.1 billion, followed by wholesale trade at S$29.3 billion. The information and communications sector contributed S$47.1 billion in nominal value-added, up from S$42.8 billion in 2024, and now accounts for 6.3 per cent of GDP compared with 5.9 per cent the previous year.
The digital economy's 5.6 per cent year-on-year growth outpaced Singapore's nominal GDP growth of 3.1 per cent, a pattern consistent with regional trends as economies layer digital infrastructure and services across existing industrial bases.
Skills Investment Targets Advanced AI
IMDA announced plans to upskill 40,000 technology professionals over the next three years through its TechSkills Accelerator programme, with a focus on advanced artificial intelligence capabilities including the deployment of agentic AI systems. The initiative reflects official recognition that current workforce capabilities may lag emerging technical requirements as enterprises move beyond foundational digitalisation.
The workforce data arrives as Singapore positions itself as a regional hub for AI development and deployment, competing with jurisdictions including Tokyo, Seoul and Hong Kong for both talent and investment. The concentration of tech employment outside traditional tech firms suggests the competitive dynamic for skilled professionals will increasingly involve banks, manufacturers and logistics operators rather than just software companies and telecommunications providers.
Whether wage growth can keep pace with demand remains an open question. The modest S$50 increase in median monthly wages suggests either a plateauing of compensation or an influx of early-career professionals that dilutes the median. The data does not break out compensation by experience level or specialisation, leaving the distribution of wage gains unclear.

Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia must integrate artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced technologies into downstream processing and manufacturing to improve efficiency and productivity and achieve its target of 8 percent economic growth, Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said.
“Moving forward, downstreaming must be increasingly technology-based by leveraging AI,” Airlangga said here on Tuesday.
He cited nickel producer PT Vale Indonesia as an example of successful AI implementation in environments that are unsafe for human workers.
The adoption of AI raised the company’s compliance rate from 89 percent to 95 percent while increasing annual nickel output by 182 tons.
“This is something only AI could achieve,” Airlangga said, adding that broader manufacturing industries are similarly benefiting from machine-to-machine learning, the Internet of Things (IoT), and Industry 4.0 automation.
Beyond industrial efficiency, the minister underscored that AI will drive demand for data center infrastructure, where Indonesia has a competitive edge due to its abundant land, energy, and water resources, as well as its large domestic market.
The push aligns with regional digital initiatives, particularly under the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which is projected to double the regional digital economy from US$1 trillion to US$2 trillion.
As ASEAN’s largest economy, accounting for roughly 40 percent of the region’s total GDP, Indonesia stands to gain significantly from this expansion.
To support the transition, the government is strengthening vocational programs and private-sector partnerships to develop local talent in AI and semiconductors.
Airlangga described the technological shift as the next phase of Indonesia’s structural economic transformation, moving the country’s main sources of value from agriculture to heavy manufacturing and ultimately toward high-value digital services.
Strengthening downstreaming, industrialization, green energy, and digitalization is key to boosting national productivity and competitiveness, the minister said, calling on the private sector to partner with the government to capitalize on these emerging industries.

articles.title: Vietnam’s lending-driven growth courts financial risks - East Asia Forum
articles.summary: Vietnam’s lending-driven growth courts financial risks  East Asia Forum
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s economy is growing at an impressive pace, but the forces sustaining that growth are becoming increasingly uneven. GDP expanded by 8 per cent in the first half of 2026, while bank credit continued to accelerate. Yet household consumption remains subdued, domestic businesses are under increasing pressure and employment gains have lagged behind output growth. Rapid credit expansion is supporting high headline growth without generating an equally broad improvement in domestic economic conditions.
This does not reflect a deliberate choice by the Vietnamese government to make high bank credit growth rate their permanent long-term financing model. The government is explicitly seeking to deepen equity and bond markets, yet the economy’s dependence on bank intermediation steadily increased from 124 per cent of GDP in 2021 to a projected 143 per cent in 2025.
Much of the domestic private sector consists of small enterprises with limited access to bond and equity markets which continue to depend heavily on banks. Policy should focus on improving credit allocation and access, ensuring that credit supports broad-based private sector development. Over time, a stronger private sector would itself create the demand needed to deepen the capital markets. Yet credit has become increasingly concentrated in large corporations, while smaller domestic firms continue to face tighter financing conditions.
In June 2026, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) introduced a special mechanism allowing lending for 18 major projects with estimated financing needs of 752 trillion dong (US$29 billion) to be excluded from standard annual credit growth limits. In July 2026, the same large private corporations proposed similar credit support for another 17 projects requiring an estimated 955 trillion dong (US$36 billion) in bank financing. These proposed financing needs illustrate the risk that scarce bank funding becomes increasingly concentrated in mega-projects intended to support double-digit growth.
Against this concentration of prospective credit demand, conditions facing the broader domestic private sector have weakened. In July 2026, new business registrations declined by 13.9 per cent year-on-year, while enterprises awaiting dissolution and completed dissolutions increased by 137 per cent and 270 per cent respectively.
In the second quarter of 2026, around 1.4 million young people aged 15–24 — 10 per cent of the youth population — were not in employment, education or training. The youth unemployment rate averaged 8.8 per cent in the first half of 2026, 0.71 percentage points higher than a year earlier. These trends demonstrate the increasingly uneven distribution of the benefits associated with rapid aggregate growth.
Rapid credit expansion is also tightening funding conditions, increasing financial stress to small firms. The SBV has maintained the refinancing rate at 4.5 per cent and the rediscount rate at 3 per cent since 2023, suggesting a supportive monetary stance. Total outstanding credit in the banking system reached 20.1 quadrillion dong (US$775 billion) in August 2026, up more than 9 per cent from the end of 2025 and outpacing deposit mobilisation, which increased by 8 per cent to 19.2 quadrillion dong (US$741 billion).
Credit expansion supports large-scale investment and near-term GDP growth, but also increases banks’ funding requirements. Competition for deposits puts upward pressure on bank funding costs, which translates into higher borrowing costs for firms and households. Smaller domestic businesses are particularly exposed, while higher interest rates restrain consumption. The same credit strategy intended to stimulate growth can weaken parts of the economy that receive less of the additional financing.
The SBV has sought to relieve funding pressures through a series of regulatory adjustments. From July 2026, it raised the maximum share of short-term funding that banks can use for medium- and long-term lending from 30 per cent to 40 per cent. It also increased the share of State Treasury term deposits recognised in the calculation of banks’ loan-to-deposit ratios from 20 per cent to 50 per cent from August 2026, allowing banks to issue more loans without breaching regulatory limits.
These measures can ease near-term funding constraints but they do not resolve the underlying funding mismatch. Greater reliance on short-term funding for long-term lending increases maturity risks, while Treasury deposits represent temporary fiscal balances that could decline as public investment disbursement accelerates. The SBV’s regulatory relief facilitates continued credit expansion in the short-term while leaving — and potentially increasing — the banking system’s exposure to liquidity and maturity risks.
Vietnam faces a structural mismatch between the long-term financing needs and a financial system still dominated by bank credit. In the near term, there is a risk that incremental credit is becoming increasingly concentrated rather than broadly supporting the economy and private sector development. This calls for a careful reassessment of the pursuit of double-digit growth. Growth targets should remain consistent with macroeconomic and financial stability, rather than becoming an overriding objective that compels the financial system to accommodate ever-higher levels of investment and leverage.
Cuong Nguyen is a retired economist. He is the former Principal Economist for Regional Economic Integration at the Asian Development Bank and former Principal Country Economist in the Viet Nam Resident Mission, Asian Development Bank.

articles.title: RI needs tech pivot to rival Vietnams economic growth: Airlangga - ANTARA News
articles.summary: RI needs tech pivot to rival Vietnams economic growth: Airlangga  ANTARA News

Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia must shift aggressively toward technology-driven industries and trade agreements to match the rapid economic growth achieved by countries like Vietnam, Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto stated.
Airlangga highlighted Vietnam’s impressive year-on-year growth of 9.95 percent in the third quarter of 2026 as a target benchmark for Indonesia, which has historically maintained an average growth rate of around 5 percent.
"If we want to catch up with Vietnam, which can reach 9 percent, we must pivot toward digitalization, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence—areas where Vietnam leveraged opportunities earlier than Indonesia," Airlangga said during an address in Jakarta on Tuesday.
Beyond technological investment, the minister attributed Vietnam's rapid momentum to its expansive Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and favorable investment climate.
While Indonesia currently operates roughly 24,000 hectares of SEZs, Vietnam has designated 2 million hectares, offering investors greater scale and policy predictability.
"They are operating on a much larger scale and are bolder. In terms of business certainty, they provide excellent service to investors," he stated.
Airlangga also highlighted Vietnam’s proactive trade strategy, noting its early execution of key international agreements such as with the European Union and favorable trade tariff terms with the United States.
However, Airlangga observed that unlike Indonesia, Vietnam lacks strong internal consumer demand—making export performance the primary driver of its economy.
"This is what drives Vietnam’s exports to grow faster than ours; since they lack a large domestic market, investors in Vietnam are compelled to focus on exports," he noted.
To capitalize on Indonesia's domestic market strength, Airlangga stressed the need to expand the industrial sector beyond natural resource downstreaming to include automotive, textiles, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), and manufacturing.
He noted that downstreaming represents only one element of a broader industrial strategy required to transform the economy.
"We need to boost these areas significantly so that the industrial sector's contribution to GDP can rise above 20 percent," Airlangga concluded.

KADIN-hosted forum examines decarbonisation, energy transition and sustainable economic development in Indonesia.
The Indonesia Sustainability Forum (ISF) 2026 opened on 6 October 2026 at Hotel Indonesia Kempinski Jakarta, with policymakers, businesses, financial institutions and sustainability organisations discussing climate action, decarbonisation and sustainable economic development. Hosted by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KADIN), the two-day forum runs from 6-7 October and addresses energy transition, green industry, sustainable finance, food systems, water security and sustainable urban development.
Mr. Anindya Novyan Bakrie, Chairman of KADIN, and Mr. Rosan Roeslani, Indonesia’s Minister of Investment and Downstream Industry and Chief Executive Officer of Danantara Indonesia, opened the forum with remarks at the Kempinski Grand Ballroom. Ms. Retno Marsudi, UN Special Envoy on Water, and Ms. Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, Under-Secretary-General and Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP), delivered keynote speeches.
The opening discussions examined energy security in the low-carbon era, followed by sessions on green industry and food systems. Speakers included Ms. Helen Clarkson OBE, Chief Executive Officer of The Climate Group; Mr. Justin Ma, Regional Head of Transition Finance and Advisory at Standard Chartered; Mr. Ashish Sharma, Executive Director of Group Sustainability at DBS Bank; Mr. Bobby Gafur Umar, President Director of PT Maharaksa Biru Energi Tbk; and Mr. Agung Wicaksono, Director of Transformation & Business Sustainability at PT Pertamina (Persero). Mr. Antonio Castellano, Partner at McKinsey & Company Singapore, moderated the energy security session.
Beyond the plenary programme, thematic discussions examined renewable energy, forestry, climate resilience, blue carbon, sustainable infrastructure and other decarbonisation issues. Knowledge partners including businesses and industry associations led these sessions, which explored policy, financing, technology and investment questions in greater depth
The programme continues on 7 October with discussions on water security, competitive and liveable cities, investment, innovation, talent and economic development. articles.title: World Bank Sees 5.2% Growth for Indonesia: What's Behind the Revision? - Tempo.co English
articles.summary: World Bank Sees 5.2% Growth for Indonesia: What's Behind the Revision?  Tempo.co English
articles.full_text:
October 6, 2026 | 03:04 pm
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The World Bank has raised its projection for Indonesia's economic growth to 5.2 percent in 2026, a 0.5 percentage point increase compared to the previous projection of 4.7 percent.
The revision is primarily driven by the impact of soaring energy prices on the Indonesian economy, which is expected to be smaller than previously anticipated.
"Growth in Indonesia is projected to remain stable at 5.2 percent in 2026 and 2027. This represents a 0.5 percentage point upgrade in the forecast for 2026, as the drag from higher energy prices has been less severe than anticipated," the World Bank wrote in its October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update report, published in Jakarta on Tuesday.
The government's policy mix is considered to have supported short-term economic growth, but at the same time contributed to larger fiscal and external imbalances.
This situation is expected to persist in the next few years, with the current account deficit projected to widen to 1.5 percent of GDP this year.
As fiscal stimulus wanes, Indonesia's medium-term economic growth is expected to become increasingly dependent on private investment. Meanwhile, inflation is projected to remain around the upper bound of the central bank's target range.
World Bank Chief Economist for Asia Franziska Lieselotte Ohnsorge said that the main driver of Indonesia's economic growth so far still relies on strong domestic demand.
According to her latest report, Indonesia's projected growth of 5.2 percent is also above the average for the East Asia and Pacific region, which is estimated at 4.5 percent.
This regional growth projection is up from the World Bank's April 2026 estimate of 4.2 percent.
Indonesia's positive projection aligns with its relatively strong economic performance in the first half of 2026. The World Bank recorded Indonesia's economy growing by 5.4 percent in the first half of 2026, up from 5.1 percent in 2025.
This growth represents the strongest two-quarter average since 2022 and primarily reflects strengthening private consumption and a surge in government spending around the turn of the year.
The World Bank stated that the growth in consumption and government spending in early 2026 was influenced by, among other factors, the earlier start of Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr, the earlier disbursement of holiday bonuses for civil servants (ASN), and the accelerated implementation of the free nutritious meal program.
Domestic economic activity fell
Despite the strong footing, domestic economic activity in Indonesia subsequently weakened.
The manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) contracted to 49.3 in August 2026, while consumer confidence fell to 116.8 in July 2026.
The World Bank also noted that the increasing deficit raises concerns regarding Indonesia's fiscal trends and sovereign debt ratings.
Market sentiment towards Indonesia deteriorated in January 2026 and was further exacerbated by rising global oil prices and shipping disruptions. Portfolio outflows reached 0.2 percent of GDP in the first quarter of 2026.
"Concerns that Indonesia would be downgraded to frontier status by the global stock index provider MSCI—triggering automatic sales from passive index funds—led to a sharp decline in the value of the rupiah and the Jakarta stock index (JCI)," the World Bank wrote in its report.
The government then responded by using foreign exchange reserves, implementing financial sector reforms, and raising the central bank's policy interest rate by a cumulative 100 basis points in May and June 2026.
These measures helped contain the impact of the weakening exchange rate on inflation.
The World Bank recorded that inflation fell from 4.8 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July 2026, partly due to fuel subsidies that restrained price increases.

articles.title: Thailand sees safe-haven appeal as global economy fragments - Pattaya Mail
articles.summary: Thailand sees safe-haven appeal as global economy fragments  Pattaya Mail
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK, Thailand – Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas says Thailand can navigate growing global economic uncertainty by pursuing an S-T-I strategy while positioning the country as a safe investment base able to trade with all sides. Ekniti said the global economic structure has changed significantly from the 1980s, when the United States, Europe and Japan accounted for around 50–60% of global GDP. Today, the world economy is more fragmented, with those three major economic powers accounting for only about 25% combined.
The shift has been accompanied by growing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and economic disputes involving major trading powers. The United States is also using tariffs against countries running trade surpluses with it, adding further uncertainty to global commerce.
Ekniti said these risks have changed what foreign investors are looking for. Rather than seeking only the lowest-cost investment destination, investors increasingly want locations that are safe and can trade with countries across different economic blocs. He said Thailand is benefiting from this trend, with investment promotion applications through the Board of Investment (BOI) reaching about 1.47 trillion baht, up almost 40% from the previous period. Electronics, printed circuit boards and semiconductor chip testing have been among the key areas attracting investment. “I have had opportunities to meet foreign investors and asked why they chose Thailand. Most said Thailand is safe and can trade with everyone because we remain neutral,” Ekniti said.
He said investment applications alone would not be enough unless Thailand could convert them into actual investment and generate benefits for the domestic economy. The government has therefore adjusted BOI rules and accelerated approvals through the Thailand FastPass programme to remove regulatory and procedural obstacles. The programme is designed to speed up investment projects and reduce approval times across several agencies. The government is also using the Skill Bridge programme to connect foreign investment with technology transfer and workforce development. The initiative involves cooperation with Thai universities to train workers, develop new skills and establish research centres that support emerging industries.
One example is the effort to attract optical transceiver manufacturers, whose equipment is important for AI and data centres. Ekniti said Thailand is being developed as a major global production base, with cooperation involving Suranaree University of Technology and Thammasat University to train and employ around 20,000–30,000 Thai engineers and workers, alongside plans for research and development facilities in Thailand. Ekniti has described the broader S-T-I strategy as Stabilize Today, Transition Now and Invest for Tomorrow, aimed at maintaining economic stability, accelerating structural and energy transition, and investing in people and technology.

articles.title: Singapore: Trusted AI Deployment Drives Innovation And Collaboration - OpenGov Asia
articles.summary: Singapore: Trusted AI Deployment Drives Innovation And Collaboration  OpenGov Asia
articles.full_text:
Singapore is positioning itself as a real-world environment for trusted and scalable artificial intelligence, with Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How highlighting the importance of safety, deployment and collaboration during a keynote address at 0G Dev Day 2026.
Speaking at the National Gallery, Tan outlined how Singapore can support AI innovation through close cooperation between researchers, enterprises and policymakers, while ensuring emerging technologies deliver practical benefits for society.
Building A Trusted AI Ecosystem
Tan said Singapore’s compact size and interconnected technology community provide advantages for AI experimentation and collaboration. He described the country as an environment where researchers, technology providers and enterprises can work closely together to develop and deploy emerging technologies.
According to Tan, trust will be central to the next stage of AI adoption. He compared AI to a powerful engine that requires confidence in both the technology and the safeguards surrounding it before it can be widely deployed.
He noted that concerns around AI safety become particularly important in sectors such as healthcare and finance, where AI-supported decisions can have significant consequences for people and organisations.
Singapore can help build confidence by bringing together researchers, technology companies, enterprises, regulators and policymakers to develop practical approaches to AI safety and responsible deployment.
Balancing Innovation With Regulation
Tan said Singapore’s approach should extend beyond rules and regulation to include practical guardrails and operational practices that support safe AI deployment.
He stressed the importance of collaboration between regulators, enterprises and technology developers in creating systems that maintain public trust while allowing innovation to progress.
This requires organisations to consider not only what AI systems can do, but also how they are deployed, monitored and governed in real-world environments.
Tan also highlighted the importance of practical action alongside broader international discussions about AI governance. By developing and applying safeguards within operational settings, organisations can build experience in managing AI risks while continuing to explore its potential.
Using Singapore As A Deployment Base
Tan acknowledged that Singapore’s domestic market is relatively small, but said this can be offset by the country’s ability to provide a connected environment for testing and deploying emerging technologies.
Companies can deploy solutions in Singapore, refine them through real-world use and build confidence before adapting them for other markets across Southeast Asia and beyond.
Tan added that bringing technology developers together with enterprises prepared to adopt new capabilities could help create new business models, products and services.
He described AI as the latest major technology wave following earlier transformations driven by the internet, digital technology, mobile technology and enterprise software. The longer-term opportunity, he said, lies in identifying the companies and technologies that will create new value, industries and employment opportunities.
Skills, Inclusion And Public Engagement
Alongside research and deployment, Tan highlighted the importance of ensuring communities can participate in and benefit from technological change.
He referenced outreach activities and workshops designed to help people become more familiar with AI tools and digital technologies. People do not necessarily need deep technical expertise to begin using AI, he said, with greater familiarity helping individuals understand how the technology can support everyday activities.
Building digital confidence and literacy will become increasingly important as AI becomes more integrated into public services, businesses and the wider economy.
Technology Supporting Broader Social Goals
Tan concluded by emphasising that technological development should remain connected to broader social and economic outcomes. He said AI should ultimately contribute to better jobs, stronger communities and an improved quality of life.
He also highlighted the potential for technology to support Singapore’s sporting community and future generations of athletes. At the same time, he stressed that technology should enhance rather than replace human endeavour, reinforcing the importance of keeping people at the centre of AI development.

articles.full_text:
BANGKOK -- BANGKOK (AP) — Laos has a new prime minister after the communist country’s National Assembly elected veteran diplomat Saleumxay Kommasith to the post, state-run media reported Tuesday.
Saleumxay, who turns 58 on Oct. 31, was elected on Monday in the Laotian capital Vientiane in a unanimous vote of 158 lawmakers who were present, the state news agency KPL said.
He is a member of the Politburo of the ruling Lao People’s Revolutionary Party and had previously served as deputy prime minister and foreign minister. Saleumxay succeeded Sonexay Siphandone, who in turn was elected the National Assembly president.
Saleumxay studied at Russia’s Moscow State Institute of International Relations and Australia’s Monash University before serving in a series of foreign ministry posts overseeing relations with Australia, the United States, the Americas, and Europe. He also served in the Lao Mission to the United Nations in New York and can speak English, Russian, and French.
His Western-oriented career is unusual for Laos, a small land-locked and impoverished country whose leaders generally have virtually no international profile aside from links with fraternal neighboring communist governments in Vietnam and China.
In a speech to the assembly after his election, Saleumxay said his government would give immediate attention to food production, infrastructure recovery, mineral management, major investment projects, tourism, revenue collection, and monetary stability, KPL reported.
A 2026 country report for Laos issued by Germany’s Bertelsmann Stiftung says the Southeast Asian nation’s economy is weak and faces challenges from overborrowing, debt obligations, a lack of reserves and currency depreciation. “The one-party state still shows no inclination toward multiparty reform,” it noted.
Laos played a major role during the Vietnam War, not only as a battleground between a royalist government and communist rebels, but also for hosting part of the Ho Chi Minh Trail, which carried supplies from communist North Vietnam to battle in the south. It consequently suffered some of the heaviest bombing per capita in history by the U.S. Air Force.
In December 1975, the communist Pathet Lao prevailed against the U.S.-backed royalist forces and took power, as did fraternal communist forces earlier that year in Vietnam and Cambodia.
Laos continues to maintain close relations with Vietnam, whose prime minister will pay a visit on Thursday. China has increasing influence, able to exercise its huge economic muscle in cementing economic and trade cooperation. As a landlocked nation, Laos is very reliant on its neighbors, also including Thailand, for trade as well as investment. Its leading export is electricity, produced by hydropower dams.

articles.title: To help the Party take root in non-state-owned enterprises - Part 1: Identifying the gaps - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: To help the Party take root in non-state-owned enterprises - Part 1: Identifying the gaps  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The growth of non-state enterprises, especially those with foreign direct investment (FDI), is creating a large workforce, with many well-trained young workers, engineers, and managers. As this private sector plays an increasingly important role in growth, the need to build Party organizations and develop political cores within enterprises becomes even more urgent. Based on the experience of Quang Ninh, the journey for Party organizations to "take root" begins with identifying potential candidates among the workforce, creating an environment for training and development, and, more importantly, enabling each Party member and each Party organization to affirm their role through their work performance and the development of the enterprise.
Sources of Party development fromnew growth poles.
Quang Ninh's economic development space is expanding rapidly, with economic zones (EZs), industrial parks (IPs), and industrial clusters playing an increasingly prominent role in attracting investment and creating jobs. Specifically, the Quang Yen coastal economic zone focuses on developing high-tech industries, processing, manufacturing, and port logistics; the Mong Cai border gate economic zone develops trade, import-export, and border logistics; and the Van Don economic zone strongly emphasizes tourism, services, logistics, and the marine economy.
Furthermore, according to the plan for 2040, Quang Ninh will have 16 industrial parks with a total area of nearly 12,887 hectares; currently, 8 industrial parks have infrastructure investment projects approved by competent authorities. The entire city has also established and expanded 20 industrial clusters with a total area of over 1,173 hectares, of which 7 have completed infrastructure and are in operation. The development of the highway network, seaports, border gates, and connecting transportation routes is creating more favorable conditions for the continued expansion of new production spaces.
Consequently, the scale of businesses has also increased rapidly. In the first nine months of 2026, Quang Ninh saw the establishment of 2,715 new businesses, bringing the total number of operating businesses to 13,778, creating an additional 23,650 jobs. Investment capital continues to flow into the industrial, service, and logistics sectors. Quang Ninh is a bright spot in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), consistently ranking among the top localities nationwide. By the end of 2025, Quang Ninh had 236 active FDI projects with a total registered capital of nearly US$16 billion; in the first nine months of 2026, the city attracted over US$1.314 billion in foreign investment.
According to Mr. Truong Manh Hung, Deputy Head of the Quang Ninh City Economic Zone Management Board, the requirement in the new phase is not only to attract more FDI capital, but more importantly, to focus on the quality of the capital flow, technology, management level, and added value that the projects bring. Quang Ninh is strongly shifting from attracting to selecting investments, while continuing to improve infrastructure, enhance the investment environment, and support projects to start production early.
As high-tech projects, processing and manufacturing industries, electronics, and logistics continue to emerge in economic zones and industrial parks, the demand for human resources is also changing. Besides direct labor, businesses increasingly need engineers, technical staff, management personnel, and young workers with professional skills, industrial work ethics, and the ability to adapt to modern technology.
This shift is clearly visible in areas with a high concentration of FDI enterprises. The Dong Mai Industrial Park currently has 22 FDI enterprises, creating jobs for over 17,000 workers; Tonly Vietnam Electronics Technology Co., Ltd. alone employs approximately 8,000 workers. In the Bac Tien Phong, Nam Tien Phong, Song Khoai, Hai Yen industrial parks, and the Hai Ha seaport, the industrial workforce is also growing, becoming more diverse in terms of occupations and skill levels.
It is within these factories, industrial parks, and new economic zones that a large source of Party development is emerging. These are skilled workers, engineers, managers, production team leaders, trade union officials, and youth union members who possess competence, expertise, discipline, and prestige within their collectives.
As the non-state economic sector expands, the demands placed on Party building work must keep pace with the shifting labor force, proactively identifying and nurturing outstanding individuals right where they work, contribute, and grow.
The gap has not kept pace with the size of the workforce.
The rapid expansion of the non-state enterprise sector is creating a noticeable gap between the size of the workforce and the coverage of Party and mass organizations. According to a review conducted in early 2026, Quang Ninh province has 5,159 non-state enterprises in operation, employing 10 or more workers. Of these, only 238 enterprises have Party organizations (approximately 4.6% of the total number of non-state enterprises), with 5,413 Party members, including 178 Party members who are business owners.
In addition, there are 169 grassroots trade unions with 40,936 members and 47 youth organizations with 3,333 members. Throughout 2025, Party organizations in this region admitted 199 new members. Compared to the scale of over 5,000 businesses, the coverage of Party organizations remains quite modest; while behind each business is a workforce that could continue to be identified, developed, and nurtured.
In Dong Mai ward, the Dong Mai Industrial Park has over 17,000 workers, but as of early August 2026, only two Party branches were established: the Party branch of Yazaki Hai Phong Vietnam Co., Ltd. in Quang Ninh and the Party branch of Tonly Vietnam Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. Yazaki has over 3,000 workers and its Party branch has 25 members. Tonly Vietnam employs approximately 8,000 workers, but when its Party branch was established in May 2026, it only had 8 members.
The scale of thousands of employees and the initial number of party members, which was only a single digit, shows that the "gap" lies not in the company lacking young people or skilled personnel, but also in its ability to identify, gather, and nurture talent.

In Lien Hoa ward, as of the end of June 2026, there were no Party organizations within businesses, despite having three large industrial parks. Specifically, the Bac Tien Phong Industrial Park has 28 businesses with 2,060 workers, and the Nam Tien Phong Industrial Park has 3 businesses with 118 workers. Nosco Shipyard Joint Stock Company employs 780 workers, has a trade union, a youth union, and 27 Party members, but these members still operate in their residential areas. This means that businesses with hundreds of workers, Party members, and even mass organizations still lack a Party organization present at their workplaces.
The case of Mr. Ha Van Long (born in 2003), residing in Trung Ban neighborhood, also illustrates this "gap." Ha Van Long works at Boltun International Co., Ltd. (Bac Tien Phong Industrial Park) - a company without a Party branch. Therefore, the efforts of this young worker are still monitored and nurtured by the Youth Union and the Party branch of his residential neighborhood.
On the occasion of National Day, September 2nd, 2026, Long, along with two other outstanding individuals, was admitted to the Party by the Trung Ban neighborhood Party branch. Ha Van Long shared: "I really hope that my workplace has a Party branch so that I can participate in Party activities at my workplace, continue to strive and contribute."
At Bac Tien Phong Industrial Park Joint Stock Company, the potential for Party membership development already exists within the enterprise, but it remains fragmented. Through a review, the Lien Hoa Ward Party Committee identified six cadres, employees, and workers of the company who are Party members but are currently active in various Party organizations in Quang Ninh and Hai Phong. Using this pool of potential members, the local Party committee encouraged Bac Tien Phong Industrial Park Joint Stock Company to establish a Party branch on July 2nd, 2026. This demonstrates that by shifting the focus from "where Party members are active" to "where Party members are working," these previously scattered resources are identified and brought together within the enterprise.
The story that Ms. Nguyen Lan Anh, Deputy Secretary of the Party Committee of Dong Mai Ward, often tells to workers reveals another aspect of recruitment efforts. During her years working in the Trade Union in Uong Bi, Ms. Lan Anh knew two drivers from Phuc Xuyen Transport Company Limited who started working at the same time, worked hard, and achieved similar results. When the company selected outstanding individuals to attend a Party awareness class, one was chosen. The other proactively sought out the Party Branch Secretary to ask why he hadn't been selected. When asked about his purpose in joining the Party, the driver replied that he wanted to contribute more and set an example for his children.
Years later, Ms. Lan Anh still remembers that story because it shows that one cannot simply assume that the number of workers who have not joined the Party has no desire to strive for advancement. Among tens of thousands of workers, some have the motivation but have not yet been discovered, some need guidance, and some Party members are working far from their workplaces. Without an organization close enough to identify them, potential Party members, even if present, can remain hidden within a factory employing thousands of people.

articles.title: Vietnam finance firm EVF plans up to $300 mln international bond issue - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam finance firm EVF plans up to $300 mln international bond issue  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
EVF General Finance Joint Stock Company (EVF) has announced plans to issue up to $300 million of bonds in international markets in 2026, seeking to diversify its funding sources and expand access to international capital.
The plan marks a new step in EVF's strategy to diversify its funding base, expand access to international financial resources, and create additional room for growth in the next phase.
Under a plan approved by EVF's board last Friday, the company expects to conduct a private placement of U.S. dollar-denominated bonds in international markets, with a maximum total face value of $300 million and maturities of at least three years.
The bonds will be non-convertible, will not carry warrants, will be unsecured and will not qualify as subordinated debt.
The offering and issuance are expected to take place in the fourth quarter of 2026, after EVF completes the required procedures and receives necessary approvals from relevant authorities, including the State Bank of Vietnam and the State Securities Commission.
Subject to meeting applicable conditions, the bonds are expected to be offered and issued in Singapore and listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX).
The actual issue size, maturity, issue price, interest rate and other transaction terms will be determined at the time of the offering based on market conditions and the relevant transaction documents.
EVF is pursuing the international bond plan as it gradually expands its operations and diversifies its funding structure.
For EVF, the planned issue is therefore not simply a fundraising transaction. It is also part of an effort to broaden its funding platform from domestic markets to international sources, in line with its development strategy and funding needs for its next phase of growth.
Under the approved plan, proceeds from the issue are expected to be used for lending to EVF's individual and corporate customers, in accordance with applicable laws and the company's funding needs from time to time.
The funds may be allocated to lending activities across various sectors of the economy, including manufacturing and processing, construction, trade, transport, energy, technology, education, healthcare and other sectors in line with regulations and actual credit demand.
As a financial institution, EVF aims to receive, manage and allocate financial resources to meet customers' funding needs. Expanding its funding sources therefore is not only about the amount raised, but also about its ability to convert those resources into credit supporting production, business operations, investment and consumption in the economy.
Ahead of the planned international bond issue, EVF has expanded relationships with various financial institutions and foreign investors, gradually diversifying its funding sources and increasing its presence in international financial markets.
In addition, after receiving approval from an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, EVF is working with government authorities and investors to conduct a private placement of shares with a maximum total face value of VND850 billion ($32.7 million).
In 2026, Moody's maintained EVF's corporate credit rating at B2 with a stable outlook, marking the sixth consecutive year the company has retained the rating. Maintaining the credit rating over several consecutive years provides an independent reference point for international partners and investors assessing EVF's credit profile.
Also in 2026, EVF continued to expand cooperation with international development finance institutions. The company received a $20 million loan from Proparco to support climate finance and small and medium-sized enterprises led or owned by women. It also signed a $15 million loan agreement with Finnfund to strengthen long-term funding and expand access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises.
An EVF management representative said: “Gradually accessing international capital markets is part of EVF's strategy to diversify funding sources and expand its financial capacity for the next phase of development. For EVF, what matters is not only gaining access to a new source of funding, but also building the capacity to receive, manage and use those resources efficiently, based on financial discipline, risk management and transparency.”
Under the approved plan, EVF has appointed Seaport Global (DIFC) Limited as the arranger, Mayer Brown Hong Kong LLP as EVF's international counsel and VTN and Associates Law Firm Co., Ltd. as its domestic counsel.
The transaction will be subject to the necessary approvals from government authorities, international market conditions at the time of the offering, and applicable regulations.
Specific information on the actual issue size, maturity, interest rate, issue price and other terms will be disclosed by EVF in accordance with regulations and the transaction timetable.
If successfully completed, the issue will provide EVF with an additional channel to connect with international investors and further diversify its funding platform.

articles.title: Singapore stocks in Q4 2026: A steady anchor in an AI-heavy world - The Business Times
articles.summary: Singapore stocks in Q4 2026: A steady anchor in an AI-heavy world  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
The positive economic backdrop should continue to support the Republic’s market for the remainder of 2026
THE Straits Times Index (STI), which tracks Singapore’s 30 largest listed companies, enters the final quarter of 2026 after a strong year-to-date performance. It closed at 5,676 on Sep 30, about 22 per cent higher than at the start of the year.
Much of the gain came in July and August. In July, the STI held steady even as technology-heavy markets in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan fell sharply amid rounds of global tech sell-offs. In August, solid first-half results from most STI companies provided another lift to the index.
The positive economic backdrop should continue to support the Singapore market for the remainder of 2026. Singapore’s economy grew 6.1 per cent in the first half of the year, prompting the government to raise its full-year growth forecast for the second time to 4.5 to 5.5 per cent. Inflation also remains contained at 2.3 per cent.
With growth firm and price pressures manageable, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has room to pursue a gradual, data-dependent appreciation path for the Singapore dollar, helping to contain the cost of imported goods. Together, solid economic growth and stable prices should provide a supportive environment for corporate earnings.
Industrials drive growth, banks provide income
Industrial companies are set to remain the main engine of the STI’s earnings growth. ST Engineering and Yangzijiang Shipbuilding have record order books, with contracts for ships, defence equipment and infrastructure already secured for years ahead. This gives investors good visibility on earnings for the next several years.
The three local banks, which make up the largest part of the index, should continue to benefit from wealth flowing into Singapore as a safe financial hub. Their interest income, which shrank as rates fell last year, is set to recover as local interest rates have edged up since May.
Together, these factors should support bank earnings for the rest of 2026 and into 2027. After a strong run, bank shares are now closer to fair value, but their dividends remain an important source of income for investors and a steady contributor to total returns.
Real estate investment trusts (Reits) are the weaker spot, as higher-for-longer interest rates continue to weigh on their payouts.
However, industrials have overtaken Reits to become the second-largest sector in the STI. With banks and industrials continuing to grow, weakness in Reits has a smaller impact on the overall index than in previous years.
Market reforms have further to run
Efforts to make Singapore’s stock market more attractive still have room to run. MAS recently appointed a third batch of Equity Market Development Programme asset managers, bringing total placements to S$5.4 billion across 14 managers and leaving S$1.1 billion of the S$6.5 billion programme still to be deployed.
A further S$20 million has been committed to support market making across around 80 small and mid-cap stocks outside the STI till 2028. Companies are also improving shareholder returns through share buybacks, while a new listing route linking the Singapore Exchange and Nasdaq went live in June.
These changes will take time to reshape the market. The benefits – including broader research coverage, more active trading and a wider choice of companies – should build gradually rather than lift the whole market at once.
This is especially true for smaller companies, which have been among the primary beneficiaries of the reforms. The share prices of many of them have risen significantly since the reforms began, making broad-based gains less likely to repeat.
From here, investors will need to be more selective, focusing on companies whose earnings can keep pace with their higher share prices.
Singapore’s place in portfolios
Based on our earnings forecasts, we expect the STI to reach 6,223 by the end of 2028. Beyond earnings growth, Singapore offers two qualities that are increasingly valuable in today’s market: diversification and income.
Global stock markets have become increasingly dominated by AI and technology companies, bringing strong growth potential but also greater volatility. The STI, made up mainly of banks, industrial companies and Reits, offers a different mix of exposures.
This was evident during the tech sell-offs since July, when many technology-heavy indices fell sharply, while the STI remained resilient and even outperformed during several periods.
Income is another attraction. With a projected dividend yield of 4 to 4.3 per cent between 2026 and 2028, the STI remains among the higher-yielding major equity markets globally.
Dividend income provides an additional source of return that is less dependent on short-term changes in market sentiment, supporting a favourable total return profile for the index.
Singapore’s investment case has therefore evolved from a rerating story into one that is increasingly supported by earnings and income. Earnings growth provides the foundation for returns, dividends add a recurring income component, while the continued rollout of market reforms leaves scope for further rerating over time.
For investors looking to diversify away from concentrated technology exposure, Singapore equities offer a differentiated combination of earnings growth, income and diversification.
The writer is a research analyst with the research and portfolio management team at FSM Global, the B2C division of iFast Financial, which is the Singapore subsidiary of iFast Corp

articles.full_text:
Thai retail giant Central Retail will invest more than VND602.5 billion ($23.18 million) to build a GO! Pleiku shopping mall in Vietnam’s central province of Gia Lai.
Nguyen Huu Que, Vice Chairman of the Gia Lai People's Committee, recently presented an investment registration certificate to Viet-Nhat Real Estate JSC. The provincial Department of Finance issued the certificate on September 25.
The company had previously been leased the land by the people's committee through a land-use rights auction to develop the project at 27 Nguyen Van Cu street, Dien Hong ward.
Viet-Nhat Real Estate was established on August 18, 2014, with its headquarters at 222 Tran Duy Hung street in Yen Hoa ward, Hanoi. The company's legal representatives are Jariya Chirathivat, a Thai national and chairwoman of the board; Olivier Bernard R. Langlet, a Belgian national and general director; and Phoom Chirathivat, a Thai national and director.
According to Langlet, CEO of Central Retail Vietnam and Viet-Nhat Real Estate, Central Retail, which entered the Vietnamese market in 2012, has invested about $1.5 billion in the country. The group now operates a retail network comprising 43 GO! hypermarkets, 48 supermarkets and more than 330 food and non-food retail stores across 26 of Vietnam's 34 provinces and cities.
Central Retail focuses on two main formats: GO! hypermarkets in medium-sized and large cities, and GO! stores in smaller cities, rural and suburban areas, combining shopping with children's entertainment and food services.
In Gia Lai, Central Retail currently operates two outlets, GO! Quy Nhon and GO! An Nhon, with combined investment of $16.54 million. The stores have contributed more than $563,000 to the state budget and created jobs for more than 200 local workers.
Project expected to boost trade in Pleiku
The GO! Pleiku shopping mall will cover nearly 1.48 hectares, with total investment of more than VND602.5 billion ($23.18 million). Of this, the investor's equity contribution will exceed VND120.5 billion ($4.64 million), while more than VND482 billion will be raised from other sources.
According to the investment documents, the project aims to invest in, build and manage a shopping mall and supermarket complex, with space for shops, kiosks, offices and other commercial activities.
It is designed to combine multiple business formats, including a general merchandise supermarket, specialty stores, branded shops, food outlets, restaurants, cinemas, entertainment facilities and children's play areas.
Under the approved schedule, the company plans to complete the building's shell and interior fit-out and put the project into operation between October 2027 and September 2028. The project will have an operating term of 50 years from the date of the land lease decision.
Gia Lai's Vice Chairman Que said Central Group's investment in a shopping mall in Pleiku signalled continued business interest in western Gia Lai and reflected the province's development strategy for trade, logistics and services.
Following the merger of Gia Lai and Binh Dinh provinces last July to form the new Gia Lai, and the relocation of the new administrative center to Quy Nhon (the capital of the former Binh Dinh province), many residents had been concerned about a slowdown in economic activity in Pleiku and western Gia Lai, Que said.
“But Central Retail's investment in a large, vibrant and modern shopping mall in Pleiku demonstrates the province's commitment to investment across all sectors and areas. I believe this is good news for residents across western Gia Lai and the Pleiku urban area,” Que said, urging the investor to begin construction soon.
Que also noted the province has many products under the One Commune One Product (OCOP) program, including around 20 products rated five-star under the program. He asked Central Retail to consider featuring high-quality OCOP products at its GO! supermarket.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Business power across Asia-Pacific is shifting, as a new generation of women leaders gains influence alongside some of the region’s most established corporate figures. Fortune today unveiled its third annual Most Powerful Women Asia list, recognizing 100 women whose leadership, business performance and influence are helping shape the region’s economic future.
At the top of the 2026 ranking, DBS Group CEO Tan Su Shan retains the No. 1 position, while Grace Wang holds at No. 2. One of the year’s most significant moves comes from technology entrepreneur Zhou Qunfei, who climbs 25 places to No. 3, underscoring the growing influence of technology among Asia’s most powerful women in business.
That shift is reflected more broadly across the ranking. Technology is the most represented sector on this year’s list, with 16 honorees, ahead of banking with 14. Their presence reflects the increasingly central role technology plays in Asia’s economy, as businesses spanning digital platforms, advanced manufacturing and other technology-driven industries grow in scale and influence.
The ranking also reveals both continuity and change in Asia’s corporate leadership. Of the 100 honorees, 76 return from last year’s list, while 24 make their debut, bringing a new cohort of leaders into the ranking alongside many of the region’s most distinguished and established business figures.
The list spans 14 markets across Asia-Pacific, with mainland China accounting for the largest number of honorees at 18, followed by Hong Kong SAR with 16 and Singapore with 12. Other markets represented include Thailand (9), India (7), Japan (6), Australia (6), Vietnam (5), Malaysia (5), South Korea (4), the Philippines (4), Taiwan region (3), Indonesia (3) and Macau SAR (2).

- Zhou Qunfei, Founder and Chairwoman, Lens Technology

- Wang Fengying, President, Xpeng Motors
