Beyond individual rankings, the list reflects the international reach of women leading some of Asia’s largest businesses. Twenty-five honourees hold global or regional leadership positions at Fortune Global 500 companies, while 23 serve as CEOs, chairs or other C-suite executives at Fortune Southeast Asia 500 companies.
"What stands out in this year’s ranking is how the landscape of business power in Asia is evolving," said Charmian Choo, Asia list Senior Manager. "We see established leaders continuing to shape some of the region’s largest companies, alongside a new generation rising through the ranks. The prominence of technology is particularly striking, reflecting the sector’s growing influence on Asia’s economy and the women increasingly at the forefront of that transformation."
Fortune evaluated candidates based on the scale and performance of their organizations, career trajectory, influence, innovation and broader societal impact.
Alongside the business ranking, Fortune also spotlights 10 exceptional women whose achievements extend beyond the corporate world, including world champions, celebrated artists, a space pioneer and changemakers in philanthropy and public policy. Their stories offer a broader perspective on the different forms of influence shaping contemporary Asia.

articles.full_text:
Myanmar’s military has launched airstrikes on camps for internally displaced people in Rakhine State, killing at least eight people and leaving more injured, according to a local ethnic rebel organization.
The Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that controls much of the state in western Myanmar, said yesterday that a Y12 aircraft bombed a displacement shelter and a nearby village in AA-controlled Ponnagyun Township, The Irrawaddy reported. One civilian was killed and two injured in the attack, it added.
This came after six were killed in an air attack on a separate displacement camp in the township on Sunday night, the AA claimed. Several more were injured in the attack, which also destroyed buildings.
The two attacks were also confirmed by the Ponnagyun Youth Association, which told Reuters that everyone killed or injured was a “displaced civilian.”
“Attacking these civilian targets with aircraft was a deliberative move,” Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and aid worker, told The Irrawaddy, adding that the camps were located far from the active combat zone in Rakhine State.
This week’s airstrikes are just the latest to take place in Rakhine, as the Myanmar armed forces attempt to claw back territory from the AA. Much of the state has fallen under the control of the AA since late 2023, when the group and its allies launched an offensive known as Operation 1027. The military has only a few precarious footholds in the state now, including the state capital Sittwe and several other coastal areas. As it has done in other parts of Myanmar, it has begun to lean heavily on its air power to punish civilian populations and stave off further losses.
The attacks came a week after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least 58, according to the AA and other local sources. In December, an attack on a hospital in Mrauk U township killed at least 30 people.
The attacks indicate that despite the efforts of the new quasi-civilian government to project a sense of stability and normalcy, the situation in much of the country is unstable. Since taking office as president in April, coup leader-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic offensive aimed at normalizing Myanmar’s relations with its neighbors. This includes the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded Myanmar from its summits since late 2021 over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan.
In a response to the September 28 attack, the Philippines, ASEAN’s current chair, said that it was “closely monitoring developments” and expressed “concern” over the attacks, Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie Hernando told Reuters on Saturday. The air strike was also condemned by U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk.
While Myanmar’s military has recently succeeded in halting the loss of territory to ethnic armed groups and other resistance factions, nearly 3.8 million people remain displaced across the country, according to the United Nations, and the central state’s hold on much of the country remains either loose or non-existent.
With the failure of a recent military offensive aimed at seizing territory around Sittwe, the Myanmar armed forces will likely compensate by relying ever more heavily on the use of air power in Rakhine State.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) have agreed to deepen bilateral co-operation across financial regulation, fintech, payment systems and capital market connectivity following a high-level meeting in Hong Kong on 2 October 2026. The discussions focused on improving cross-border financial infrastructure, supporting digital innovation and strengthening regional resilience. According to the official announcement, the two central banks also explored opportunities to expand local currency usage and strengthen Islamic finance collaboration.
New areas of fintech and digital asset collaboration
A key outcome of the meeting was the establishment of a joint policy-focused workstream on compliant cross-border stablecoin use cases between Hong Kong and Malaysia. The initiative will examine how digital assets and related payment technologies could support cross-border financial transactions while remaining aligned with regulatory requirements in both jurisdictions.
The two authorities also agreed to expand policy and regulatory exchanges on tokenisation and digital money. This work builds on wider regional efforts to improve digital financial infrastructure, including initiatives linked to regional fintech collaboration and emerging cross-border payment frameworks.
Officials discussed opportunities for knowledge sharing on data-driven applications such as Commercial Data Interchange and CargoX. These platforms are intended to improve trade finance access for small and medium-sized enterprises by enabling more efficient data exchange between financial institutions and trade participants. The discussions align with broader developments in digital trade connectivity initiatives designed to support regional commerce.
Focus on cyber resilience and payment infrastructure
The HKMA and BNM also agreed to establish mechanisms aimed at strengthening cross-border cyber resilience and improving anti-scam and anti-fraud co-operation. The move reflects increasing attention among financial regulators on operational resilience and cross-border responses to cyber threats affecting payment systems and digital financial services.
Another area of collaboration involves promoting broader use of local currencies in bilateral trade and investment. The authorities said they would enhance connectivity between the Real Time Gross Settlement systems in Hong Kong and Malaysia to improve payment efficiency and support regional financial integration.
The initiative complements wider efforts to strengthen digital public infrastructure and improve resilience across financial ecosystems in the region.
Capital market and Islamic finance initiatives
The two central banking institutions also explored the possibility of linking Hong Kong’s Central Moneymarkets Unit with Malaysia’s Real Time Electronic Transfer of Funds and Securities System (RENTAS). Such a connection could support greater interoperability between market infrastructures and facilitate cross-border investment activities.
In addition, the authorities agreed to deepen collaboration on Islamic finance market development and connectivity. Areas identified for further co-operation include industry engagement, talent development, sustainable finance and cross-border investment support.
“We are delighted to welcome the BNM delegation to Hong Kong. This high-level meeting marks an important milestone in deepening collaboration between our two institutions to support financial market development and economic growth. Based on our shared vision, we look forward to advancing co-operation in fintech and digital asset innovation, improving the efficiency of cross-border local currency transactions, strengthening market connectivity, and fostering the growth of the Islamic finance market.” Mr Eddie Yue, Chief Executive, Hong Kong Monetary Authority
The meeting reflects continuing efforts by Asian financial authorities to strengthen regional financial integration while responding to rapid developments in digital finance, cybersecurity and payment modernisation. The co-operation measures outlined by the HKMA and BNM are expected to support closer policy coordination and operational connectivity between the two financial systems.

articles.title: VN-Index faces the October slump: Waiting for a new equilibrium zone. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: VN-Index faces the October slump: Waiting for a new equilibrium zone.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| The preferred strategy is risk management, avoiding bottom-fishing, and waiting for the market to establish a new equilibrium zone. | 
 The macroeconomic outlook is brighter, but capital flows remain cautious.
 According to MBS, the Vietnamese stock market entered the new trading week in a rather unusual state: positive signals from the macroeconomic foundation and policies have not been adequately reflected on the trading screen. The VN-Index has fallen for two consecutive weeks after being upgraded to FTSE standards, while liquidity remains low and selling pressure is still widespread across many stock groups.
 At the end of last week, the VN-Index closed at 1,737.71 points, down 47.4 points, or 2.66%. VIC was the stock exerting the biggest downward pressure, deducting 12.9 points from the index, followed by LPB with 3.9 points and STB with 3.2 points. With this performance, the VN-Index has fallen 2.6% since the beginning of the year, while global stock indices have risen 12.4%.
 The downward pressure wasn't limited to large-cap stocks. The VN30 fell 3.2%, Midcap lost 3.4%, and Smallcap declined 1.5%. Market breadth clearly favored declines, with only 33% of stocks showing gains.
 Differentiation remains evident in some sectors. Insurance increased by 7.6%, natural rubber by 3%, and seafood by 1.7%. Conversely, stocks decreased by 6.1%, residential real estate by 5.2%, and technology by 4.1%.
 The more noteworthy point lies in the cash flow. Average market liquidity reached VND 17,300 billion, similar to the previous week; however, matched order liquidity decreased by 1.5%, to VND 13,100 billion.
 On a monthly basis, liquidity in September fell to its lowest level since the beginning of the year, down 5% from August and 53% year-on-year, to VND 17,700 billion. Since the beginning of the year, average market liquidity has reached VND 25,300 billion, 12.5% lower than the 2025 average and down 14.4% year-on-year.
 Foreign capital flows have not yet shown signs of reversal. Foreign investors sold a net 1,660 billion VND last week. In September alone, the net selling value reached 4,655 billion VND; the cumulative figure from the beginning of the year is 98,440 billion VND, equivalent to approximately 3.77 billion USD. Previously, in 2025, foreign investors recorded a record net selling of 135,329 billion VND, approximately 5.2 billion USD, marking the third consecutive year of net selling and the fifth year of net selling in six years.
 During the week, foreign investors net bought SBT shares worth VND 159 billion, FRT shares worth VND 121 billion, and MSN shares worth VND 90 billion, but net sold PNJ shares worth VND 1,459 billion, HDB shares worth VND 936 billion, and VPB shares worth VND 559 billion. Securities companies' proprietary trading desks, however, net bought HDB shares worth VND 1,467 billion, VPB shares worth VND 906 billion, and GMD shares worth VND 155 billion; while net selling LPB shares worth VND 511 billion, TCB shares worth VND 297 billion, and EIB shares worth VND 101 billion.
 The cautious flow of funds is occurring while the domestic economy shows many positive signs. GDP growth for the first nine months of 2026 is projected at 9.01%. Circular 50/2026/TT-NHNN, amending and supplementing Circular 22/2019/TT-NHNN, is considered to have a positive impact on listed banks. If the LCR and NSFR ratios are applied to management early, raising the LDR ceiling from 85% to 95% could reduce liquidity pressure and create more room for lending.
 However, these positive signals need time to translate into an impact on the market. In the short term, low liquidity and cautious sentiment remain prevalent as several macroeconomic balances need to be continuously monitored.
 The average CPI for the first nine months increased by 4.52% year-on-year due to fluctuations in the prices of gasoline, food, and construction materials. Total import and export turnover reached US$888.02 billion, an increase of 30.4%, but the economy recorded a trade deficit of US$19.42 billion due to a 36.7% increase in imports, despite a trade surplus of US$1.27 billion in September alone.
 In addition, there are issues such as uneven disbursement of public investment across localities, difficulties for businesses in accessing capital, and pressure from exchange rates and interest rates from the external environment. Therefore, the improvement of the macroeconomic foundation does not necessarily mean that cash flow in the stock market can immediately return to a positive state.
 October and the pressure from seasonal factors.
 International markets have also failed to provide truly favorable support. US stocks rose at the end of the week after weaker-than-expected jobs data increased expectations that the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting. The US non- farm payrolls added only 29,000 jobs in September, significantly lower than the forecast of 90,000. The August jobs figure was also revised down from 162,000 to 133,000, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%.
 Following this data, the interest rate futures market is betting at a 78% probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged in October. However, the likelihood of the Fed raising interest rates at its December meeting remains at 86%.
 Overall for the week, the Nasdaq rose 0.5%, the S&P 500 was nearly unchanged, while the Dow Jones fell 1.3%. Pressure stemmed from concerns about persistent inflation, prolonged high interest rates, and rising US Treasury yields. Yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds both reached their highest levels since 2002.
 In the commodities market, spot gold prices fell about 3.4% this week, pressured by rising bond yields and a stronger US dollar, after a 2.1% drop the previous week. Brent crude oil still ended the week above $100 a barrel, up 0.11%; WTI crude oil fell 1.6%.
 In this context, seasonality is becoming a notable variable for the VN-Index. Statistics from the past 10 years show that October has performed unfavorably, with an average decline of over 2%. Notably, for four consecutive years since 2022, the market has declined in this month.
 The seasonal signals are even more noteworthy considering that in September, despite the market experiencing a significant upgrade, the VN-Index still fell by 63.5 points, or 3.5%.
 From a technical perspective, the VN-Index has now lost the MA20, MA50, MA100, and MA200 moving averages. According to the strategy report, this has caused the uptrend formed since the end of July to shift to a downtrend.
 Low liquidity has led to a more cautious technical outlook. The VN-Index remains above 1,720 points, but the risk of losing the 1,720 or 1,700 point support level is considered quite high. The next support zone is identified in the 1,660-1,680 point area.
 From a longer-term perspective, seasonality suggests that October is the worst-performing month of the year before the market enters the final two months; November, on the other hand, is the second-best performing month. However, seasonal statistics are only one variable in the current picture, alongside liquidity, technical trends, and money flow dynamics.
 Don't rush to buy at the bottom when the market hasn't stabilized yet.
 FTSE Russell's upgrade of the Vietnamese stock market to a Secondary Emerging Market is a long-term supporting factor. Along with this, the plan to further refine the legal framework for the market creates additional expectations for institutional reforms.
 According to the report, at the government press conference on October 3rd, Deputy Minister of Finance Nguyen Duc Chi stated that the Ministry of Finance will submit to the National Assembly for approval the Law amending and supplementing a number of articles of the Securities Law at the October 2026 session.
 The combination of short-term economic support policies such as public investment, reduced capital costs, and tax incentives with long-term institutional reforms is expected to lay the foundation for growth and strengthen capital confidence in the next cycle.
 However, for investors, the immediate concern remains risk management. The VN-Index is only about 0.6% away from the 1,720-point support level, while several key stock groups have broken through their respective support levels, including securities, banking, residential real estate, construction materials, and food. In this situation, the recommended strategy is to avoid bottom-fishing or opening new positions in these stock groups.
 This is especially important to note when the weakness is not only reflected in the index but also appears simultaneously in breadth, liquidity, and multiple leading groups. A dip under conditions of strong cash flow could create an opportunity for restructuring, but when liquidity falls to low levels and the technical trend shifts to bearish, identifying a short-term bottom becomes more difficult.
 Current cash flow tends to concentrate, seeking opportunities in commodity stocks that benefit from price cycles or defensive companies with consistent dividend streams.
 Thus, the key point of the current market is the time lag between long-term supporting factors and short-term risks. GDP growth, changes in banking policy, market upgrades, and legal reforms may lay the groundwork for the next cycle, but they are not enough to immediately reverse the cautious trend in capital flows.
 For the VN-Index, the question this week is not just whether the 1,720-point level will hold. More importantly, will the market find a reliable equilibrium zone where selling pressure subsides and liquidity begins to improve? Until those signals become clearer, managing portfolio weight, limiting bottom-fishing, and patiently waiting for a new equilibrium zone remain priorities in short-term strategies.

articles.full_text:
JAKARTA: Authorities in Indonesia have arrested 11 people believed to be linked to terrorist networks in a series of operations carried out across six provinces since Oct 2.
In a statement on Sunday (Oct 4), the police counterterrorism force Special Detachment 88 (Densus 88) spokesman Mayndra Eka Wardhana said that the suspects were arrested in raids across West Java, Central Java, Central Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, Riau, and North Maluku provinces.
The 11 were aged between 22 and 52. They were identified by Densus 88 by their initials: HN (43), SM alias NM (52), HA (45), YDKAP (22), S (49), A (32), CG (29), J (36), MF (37), AF (26) and MW (42).
"The suspects are believed to be affiliated with Daulah Islamiyah and other terrorist networks," Wardhana was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
According to reports, Daulah Islamiyah is widely used to describe local extremist factions aligned with Islamic State ideology.
Wardhana on Sunday said that the arrests were followed by a series of investigations, including search operations, the seizure and examination of evidence and the questioning of witnesses and suspects.
Early investigations found purported links between the 11 suspects despite their operations spanning different provinces across Indonesia.
The suspects, Wardhana said, played various roles within their networks, including network consolidation, training, propaganda dissemination, direct and online recruitment, and planning of terrorist acts.
"One of the schemes uncovered involves online meetings that virtually connected supporters of Daulah Islamiyah from several regions," he said.
News outlet Kompas reported Wardhana as saying that there were also indications that some of the suspects had undergone training.
"From physical training, shooting, and other training activities related to terrorism militancy," he said.
Wardhana stressed that the law enforcement measures undertaken by Densus 88 form part of police efforts to mitigate the risk of terrorist acts by disrupting propaganda activities, recruitment, indoctrination, and training that could lead to violence.
Earlier in May, the counterterrorism force had arrested eight suspected terrorists linked to the Islamic State-affiliated Jamaah Ansharut Daulah network in Central Sulawesi.
Preliminary investigations then found that the eight had allegedly spread extremist propaganda through social media posts, videos, and other content linked to radicalism and terrorism.
